title: External Commerce Provider Integrations
readerIntent: Learn the reusable pattern for integrating payment gateways, delivery partners, warehouses, ERPs, and other commerce providers.
priorKnowledge: Read payment, delivery, inventory, and checkout pages.
owner: Commerce integration and owning capability teams
summary: External integrations should use method/mode configuration, provider registries, provider policy services, adapters, secure credentials, idempotency, workflows, and reconciliation instead of framework edits or UI-only workarounds.

sections.heading: Provider integration pattern
paragraphs: Most enterprise commerce systems integrate with external services: payment gateways, tax engines, shipping carriers, warehouse management systems, ERPs, fraud engines, customer notification platforms, marketplaces, and analytics providers.

The same architectural pattern should repeat everywhere: business-facing method or mode, provider registration, provider policy, provider adapter, secure connector, normalized evidence, retry, reconciliation, and Axis visibility.

sections.heading: Layered responsibilities
items: Method or mode: business choice such as Card, Cash on Delivery, Standard Delivery, Pickup, or Backorder Approval.
Provider: executable implementation such as Stripe, CyberSource, DHL, Aramex, SAP ERP, Oracle WMS, or customer adapter.
Provider policy: decides which provider and action are allowed for the current context.
Adapter: translates Nodics commands into provider-specific API calls or file exchanges.
Connector: owns transport, credentials, endpoints, timeouts, retries, TLS, and secret access.
Evidence model: records normalized provider result, external reference, status, correlation id, and reconciliation state.
Workflow: coordinates long-running human/system tasks after the immediate pipeline completes.
Axis metadata: exposes safe operational visibility and authorized lifecycle actions.

sections.heading: Configuration-first does not mean code in properties
paragraphs: Configuration should describe what is enabled, what codes exist, which provider is mapped, and which limits or feature flags apply. It should not become a bulky service implementation.

Runtime decisions, provider aggregation, protocol handling, normalization, and policy evaluation belong in services, adapters, utilities, and workflow actions. Customer modules can replace or extend those services without editing framework files.

sections.heading: Secure integration checklist
items: No provider secrets in content, schema records, generated documentation, browser JavaScript, or Axis responses.
Use tenant and enterprise scope on all provider registrations and business methods/modes.
Use idempotency keys for money movement, inventory commitment, label creation, shipment booking, and external state-changing calls.
Validate webhook or callback signatures before changing internal state.
Normalize provider statuses into Nodics statuses and retain raw payload only in protected evidence storage if required.
Set timeouts, retry limits, circuit breaker policy, and fallback behavior per provider.
Record correlation identifiers across pipeline, workflow, provider call, audit, logs, and Axis detail views.
Separate permissions for view, execute, retry, reconcile, cancel, refund, dispatch, and admin configuration.

sections.heading: Integration lifecycle
items: Discover provider capabilities, required credentials, supported operations, callback model, rate limits, sandbox mode, production mode, and certification rules.
Model the business method/mode and provider registration in backend configuration or schema as appropriate.
Implement provider policy and adapter services in the owning module or a customer extension module.
Add contract tests using sandbox/fake providers before connecting production credentials.
Expose safe provider state, health, and lifecycle actions in Axis through backend-driven metadata.
Document setup, customization, failure modes, recovery, audit, and operations for business users and developers.
Run staging certification, load testing, failure testing, idempotency replay testing, and rollback planning before production enablement.

sections.heading: Examples
items: Stripe card provider: Card method remains the same; provider policy selects Stripe for selected enterprises and currencies; adapter implements authorize/capture/refund; reconciliation reads Stripe events.
PayPal wallet provider: Wallet method maps to PayPal provider; adapter handles redirect or tokenized approval; webhook validates final capture status.
DHL delivery provider: Standard or Express Delivery maps to DHL in covered zones; adapter quotes services, creates labels, tracks parcels, and reconciles exceptions.
Local fleet provider: Local Delivery maps to a customer module adapter; workflow can assign driver, schedule delivery, record proof, and trigger notifications.
ERP credit provider: Account Credit method maps to ERP provider; adapter checks credit limit and posts invoice evidence asynchronously.

sections.heading: Anti-patterns
items: Putting provider business logic into `properties.js` instead of services/adapters.
Letting Axis call external payment or delivery providers directly.
Hard-coding Stripe, PayPal, CyberSource, DHL, or any partner into generic checkout logic.
Using provider status as authoritative without matching tenant, enterprise, order, amount, currency, method, provider, and idempotency evidence.
Creating duplicate payment, stock, shipment, or order state in customer modules instead of extending the owning capability.
